```{r}
#| label: setup
#| message: false
library(ars)
```

Monte Carlo integration estimates $E_f[a(\theta)] = \int a(\theta) f(\theta)\,d\theta$ from
iid draws $\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_n \sim f$. The catch is the sampling step
itself: R has built-in samplers for standard families, but a posterior
$f(\theta) \propto L(\theta)\pi(\theta)$ is typically known only up to a
constant, and there is no generic way to draw from it directly. **Rejection
sampling** solves this by producing *exact* iid draws from $f$ using draws
from an easier distribution $g$, following the recipe *reject, reweight,
repeat*.

## The Envelope and the Algorithm

### The envelope condition

Suppose we can find a function $g(x)$ such that

- $g(x) \ge f(x)$ for every $x$ — an **envelope** of $f$, and
- we can sample from the normalized density $g(x)/A_g$, where
  $A_g = \int g(x)\,dx$.

Neither $f$ nor $g$ needs to be normalized: $f$ may be an unnormalized
posterior with unknown area $A_f = \int f(x)\,dx$, and $g$ a scaled density
$M\,g_0(x)$ for a sampler $g_0$ we already have. We will see that the
acceptance rate of the algorithm is $A_f/A_g$. So the design problem is
finding a $g$ that is both easy to sample and close to $f$.

### Uniform points under a curve

Rejection sampling rests on one fact about points spread uniformly under the
graph of a function. For a function $h \ge 0$ with finite area
$A_h = \int h(x)\,dx$, write the region under its graph as
$$
S_h = \{(x, v): 0 < v < h(x)\}.
$$
The area of $S_h$ is $A_h$, so a point $(X, V)$ **uniform on $S_h$** has joint
density $1/A_h$ on $S_h$ and $0$ elsewhere.

::: {#thm-uniform-under-curve}
## Uniform under a curve

Let $h \ge 0$ with $0 < A_h = \int h(x)\,dx < \infty$.

(a) If $(X, V)$ is uniform on $S_h$, then the marginal density of $X$ is
    $h(x)/A_h$.

(b) Conversely, if $X$ has density $h(x)/A_h$ and, given $X$,
    $V \sim \text{Unif}(0, h(X))$, then $(X, V)$ is uniform on $S_h$.
:::

::: {.proof}
(a) Integrate the joint density over $v$. For fixed $x$, the point $(x, v)$
lies in $S_h$ exactly when $0 < v < h(x)$, so
$$
p_X(x) = \int_0^{h(x)} \frac{1}{A_h}\,dv = \frac{h(x)}{A_h}.
$$

(b) The joint density is the marginal of $X$ times the conditional of $V$
given $X$:
$$
p(x, v) = \frac{h(x)}{A_h}\cdot\frac{1}{h(x)}\,\mathbb{1}\{0<v<h(x)\}
= \frac{1}{A_h}\,\mathbb{1}\{(x, v) \in S_h\},
$$
which is the uniform density on $S_h$.
:::

Part (a) says the density of $X$ at $x$ is proportional to the **height** of
the region at $x$: a tall column holds more points than a short one. Part (b)
gives a way to fill $S_h$ uniformly using a sampler for $h/A_h$.
@fig-uniform-under-curve illustrates both parts with the Laplace-shaped
function $g(x) = e^{1/2-|x|}$, which has area $A_g = 2e^{1/2}$.

```{r}
#| label: fig-uniform-under-curve
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 3.5
#| fig-cap: "Illustrates the theorem that a point uniform under the graph of g has marginal density proportional to g, and conversely.
#|   Left: uniform points in the box $[-6,6]\\times[0, e^{1/2}]$, kept when they fall under
#|   $g(x) = e^{1/2-|x|}$, so they are uniform on $S_g$. Middle: the histogram of their
#|   $x$-coordinates matches $g(x)/A_g$, as in part (a). Right: points made the other way, by
#|   drawing $X$ from $g/A_g$ and then $V$ uniform on $(0, g(X))$, as in part (b). They fill $S_g$
#|   in the same uniform way as the left panel."
g_demo <- function(x) exp(0.5 - abs(x))
A_g <- 2 * exp(0.5)                      # area under g
xs <- seq(-6, 6, length.out = 500)
### sampler for the normalized g, a Laplace(0, 1) density, by inverse CDF
rlaplace <- function(n) { u <- runif(n); ifelse(u < 0.5, log(2 * u), -log(2 * (1 - u))) }

set.seed(2)
### part (a): uniform points in a box, kept if under g
nb <- 30000
xb <- runif(nb, -6, 6); vb <- runif(nb, 0, exp(0.5))
keep <- vb < g_demo(xb); xa <- xb[keep]; va <- vb[keep]
### part (b): X ~ g / A_g, then V | X ~ Unif(0, g(X))
nshow <- 800
xr <- rlaplace(nshow); vr <- runif(nshow) * g_demo(xr)

par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 2.2, 1))
plot(xs, g_demo(xs), type = "l", lwd = 3, col = "steelblue", ylim = c(0, 1.7),
     xlab = "x", ylab = "v", main = "(a) uniform on S_g, from a box")
points(xa[1:nshow], va[1:nshow], pch = 19, cex = 0.45, col = adjustcolor("black", 0.6))
hist(xa, breaks = seq(-6, 6, by = 0.3), freq = FALSE, col = "grey75", border = "white",
     xlab = "x", main = "(a) histogram of X vs g(x) / A_g")
lines(xs, g_demo(xs) / A_g, lwd = 3, col = "steelblue")
plot(xs, g_demo(xs), type = "l", lwd = 3, col = "steelblue", ylim = c(0, 1.7),
     xlab = "x", ylab = "v", main = "(b) X ~ g / A_g, V | X ~ Unif(0, g(X))")
points(xr, vr, pch = 19, cex = 0.45, col = adjustcolor("black", 0.6))
```

### The algorithm in two forms

**Form 1 (ratio form).** For each draw needed, repeat until acceptance:

1. Draw $X \sim g(x)/A_g$.
2. Draw $U \sim \text{Unif}(0,1)$.
3. If $U < f(X)/g(X)$, accept $X$; otherwise return to step 1.

**Form 2 (geometric form).** For each draw needed, repeat until acceptance:

1. Draw $X \sim g(x)/A_g$.
2. Draw $V \sim \text{Unif}(0, g(X))$, e.g. $V = U\,g(X)$ with
   $U \sim \text{Unif}(0,1)$.
3. If $V < f(X)$, i.e. the point $(X, V)$ lies in $S_f$, accept $X$;
   otherwise return to step 1.

The two forms are the same algorithm, since with $V = U\,g(X)$,
$$
V < f(X) \iff U < \frac{f(X)}{g(X)}.
$$
Form 1 is how the sampler is usually coded. Form 2 explains why it works,
as shown next. Both evaluate $f$ and $g$ only at the proposed point, so
unknown normalizing constants in $f$ (and in $g$) do not matter, as long as
the functions actually used satisfy $g \ge f$.

### Why the retained points have density $f$

By part (b) of @thm-uniform-under-curve, steps 1–2 of Form 2 make $(X, V)$
uniform on $S_g$. Because $g \ge f$, the region $S_f$ lies inside $S_g$.
Step 3 keeps the point only when it lands in $S_f$. So for any set
$B \subseteq S_f$,
$$
P\{(X, V) \in B \mid \text{accept}\}
= \frac{P\{(X, V) \in B\}}{P\{(X, V) \in S_f\}}
= \frac{\text{area}(B)/A_g}{A_f/A_g}
= \frac{\text{area}(B)}{A_f}.
$$
This says a retained $(X, V)$ is **uniform on $S_f$**. By part (a) of
@thm-uniform-under-curve with $h = f$, the retained $X$ has density
$f(x)/A_f$, the normalized target. The draw is exact, not approximate.

The same calculation gives the cost. Each proposal is accepted with
probability
$$
P(\text{accept}) = P\{(X, V) \in S_f\} = \frac{A_f}{A_g},
$$
the ratio of the two areas. Proposals are independent, so the number needed
per accepted draw is geometric with mean $A_g/A_f$. A tight envelope wastes
few proposals and a loose one wastes many.

@fig-envelope-scatter shows the whole picture for the standard normal target
$f(x) = e^{-x^2/2}$ under the same Laplace envelope $g$. Here $A_f =
\sqrt{2\pi} \approx 2.507$ and $A_g = 2e^{1/2} \approx 3.297$, so about
$76\%$ of proposals are accepted.

```{r}
#| label: fig-envelope-scatter
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4.4
#| fig-cap: "Illustrates the rejection sampling algorithm: candidate points are drawn uniformly under an envelope and kept when they fall under the target density.
#|   Left: target $f(x)=e^{-x^2/2}$ (unnormalized standard normal) under
#|   its Laplace envelope $g(x) = e^{1/2-|x|}$, with the two areas shaded.
#|   Right: 600 candidate points drawn uniformly under $g$; the accepted ones
#|   (red, under $f$ too) are uniformly distributed under $f$, so their
#|   $x$-coordinates are draws from the normalized $f$."
f_demo <- function(x) exp(-x^2 / 2)
xs <- seq(-6, 6, length.out = 500)

par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
plot(xs, g_demo(xs), type = "n", ylim = c(0, 1.75), xlab = "x", ylab = "")
polygon(c(xs, rev(xs)), c(g_demo(xs), rep(0, 500)), col = adjustcolor("steelblue", 0.3), border = NA)
polygon(c(xs, rev(xs)), c(f_demo(xs), rep(0, 500)), col = adjustcolor("firebrick", 0.4), border = NA)
lines(xs, g_demo(xs), col = "steelblue", lwd = 3); lines(xs, f_demo(xs), col = "firebrick", lwd = 3)
legend("topright", bty = "n", fill = adjustcolor(c("steelblue", "firebrick"), 0.35), border = NA,
       legend = c("area under envelope g", "area under target f"))

set.seed(1)
N <- 600
xp <- rlaplace(N); vp <- runif(N) * g_demo(xp); acc <- vp < f_demo(xp)
plot(xs, g_demo(xs), type = "l", lwd = 3, col = "steelblue", ylim = c(0, 1.75), xlab = "x", ylab = "v")
lines(xs, f_demo(xs), lwd = 3, col = "firebrick")
points(xp[!acc], vp[!acc], pch = 4, col = adjustcolor("gray40", 0.7), cex = 0.7)
points(xp[acc], vp[acc], pch = 19, col = adjustcolor("firebrick", 0.7), cex = 0.7)
legend("topright", bty = "n", pch = c(19, 4), col = c("firebrick", "gray40"),
       legend = c(sprintf("accepted (%d)", sum(acc)), sprintf("rejected (%d)", sum(!acc))))
```

## Example 1: Sampling a Normal from a Laplace Envelope

The figure above already uses a concrete, closed-form example worth stating
in full, because it is simple enough to check every claim exactly.

**Target.** The unnormalized standard normal density
$$
f(x) = e^{-x^2/2}, \qquad x \in \mathbb{R}, \qquad A_f = \sqrt{2\pi}.
$$

**Envelope.** A scaled Laplace (double-exponential) density
$$
g(x) = e^{1/2 - |x|} = 2e^{1/2}\,g_0(x), \qquad g_0(x) = \tfrac12 e^{-|x|},
\qquad A_g = 2e^{1/2}.
$$
The normalized envelope $g_0$ is the standard Laplace density, which is
sampled by inversion (`rlaplace` above).

::: {.proof}
**$g \ge f$ for every $x$.** Compare the logs:
$$
\log g(x) - \log f(x) = \tfrac12 - |x| + \tfrac{x^2}{2}
= \tfrac12\big(|x|^2 - 2|x| + 1\big) = \tfrac12\big(|x| - 1\big)^2 \ \ge\ 0,
$$
with equality exactly at $|x| = 1$, where the two curves in the figure touch.
The constant $e^{1/2}$ is the smallest that works: with $e^{a - |x|}$ the gap
is $\tfrac12(|x|-1)^2 + a - \tfrac12$, which is negative at $|x| = 1$ when
$a < \tfrac12$.
:::

The exact acceptance rate is
$$
P(\text{accept}) = \frac{\int f(x)\,dx}{\int g(x)\,dx}
 = \frac{\sqrt{2\pi}}{2e^{1/2}} \approx 0.760.
$$

```{r}
#| label: tbl-rnorm-reject
#| tbl-cap: "Verifies the rejection sampler for the normal distribution by comparing its acceptance rate and sample moments with theory.
#|   Theoretical vs. simulated acceptance rate and sample moments for the Laplace-envelope normal sampler."
rnorm_reject <- function(n) {
    out <- numeric(0); tries <- 0
    while (length(out) < n) {
        m <- n - length(out)
        x <- rlaplace(m); tries <- tries + m
        out <- c(out, x[runif(m) < f_demo(x) / g_demo(x)])
    }
    list(x = out, acceptance = n / tries)
}
set.seed(2)
res <- rnorm_reject(2e5)
knitr::kable(data.frame(
    quantity = c("acceptance rate", "sample mean", "sample sd"),
    theoretical = c(sqrt(2 * pi) / (2 * sqrt(exp(1))), 0, 1),
    simulated = c(res$acceptance, mean(res$x), sd(res$x))
), digits = 4)
```

Roughly 3 in 4 proposals are kept — a tight, efficient envelope, and the
benchmark against which the next example's Cauchy envelope should be judged.

[]{#rejection-app}A [shinylive app](../../shinylive_apps/app_rejection.html) shows how the tightness of the envelope determines the efficiency of rejection sampling: a looser envelope still gives exact draws but rejects more of them.

## Example 2: Sampling a Gamma Distribution

The Laplace envelope above was designed to match a normal target. A
different target needs a different envelope. Here is one built for
$\text{Gamma}(\alpha, 1)$ with $\alpha > 1$. Write $m = \alpha - 1 > 0$ for
the mode and $c = 2\alpha - 1 = 2m + 1$.

**Target.** The unnormalized Gamma density (the kernel, without $1/\Gamma(\alpha)$)
$$
f(x) = x^{\alpha-1}e^{-x} = x^m e^{-x}, \qquad x > 0,
$$
with area $A_f = \Gamma(\alpha)$ and maximum $f(m) = m^m e^{-m}$ at the mode.

**Envelope.** A Cauchy-shaped curve centred at the mode, scaled to touch $f$
there:
$$
g(x) = \frac{m^m e^{-m}}{1 + (x - m)^2/c}, \qquad x \in \mathbb{R}.
$$
Normalized, $g$ is the density of $m + \sqrt{c}\,C$ with $C$ standard Cauchy,
so sampling $g$ needs only `rcauchy`. Its area is
$A_g = m^m e^{-m}\,\pi\sqrt{c}$. The heavy Cauchy tails, decaying like
$x^{-2}$, are what let $g$ stay above the exponentially decaying $f$ for
large $x$. A normal-shaped envelope would eventually fall below it.

::: {.proof}
**$g \ge f$ for every $x > 0$.** For $x \le 0$ there is nothing to show,
since $f = 0$ there. For $x > 0$ consider the log gap
$$
D(x) = \log g(x) - \log f(x) = m\log m - m - \log\!\Big(1 + \frac{(x-m)^2}{c}\Big) - m\log x + x.
$$
Clearly $D(m) = 0$. Differentiating,
$$
D'(x) = 1 - \frac{m}{x} - \frac{2(x-m)}{c + (x-m)^2}
= (x - m)\left[\frac{1}{x} - \frac{2}{c + (x-m)^2}\right]
= \frac{(x-m)\,\big[c + (x-m)^2 - 2x\big]}{x\,\big(c + (x-m)^2\big)}.
$$
With $c = 2m + 1$ the bracket is a perfect square:
$c + (x-m)^2 - 2x = (x-m)^2 - 2(x-m) + 1 = (x - m - 1)^2 \ge 0$. So
$$
D'(x) = \frac{(x-m)(x-m-1)^2}{x\,\big(c + (x-m)^2\big)},
$$
which has the sign of $x - m$. Hence $D$ decreases on $(0, m)$ and increases
on $(m, \infty)$, its minimum is $D(m) = 0$, and $D(x) \ge 0$, i.e.
$g(x) \ge f(x)$, for all $x > 0$. This also shows where the scale
$c = 2\alpha - 1$ comes from: it is the value that turns the bracket into a
square.
:::

The acceptance rate is therefore
$$
P(\text{accept}) = \frac{A_f}{A_g} = \frac{\Gamma(\alpha)}{\pi\sqrt{2\alpha-1}\;(\alpha-1)^{\alpha-1}e^{-(\alpha-1)}}.
$$
It is $e/(\pi\sqrt 3) \approx 0.50$ at $\alpha = 2$, and by Stirling's formula
it rises to $1/\sqrt{\pi} \approx 0.564$ as $\alpha \to \infty$.

```{r}
#| label: gamma-envelope-fns
### log Gamma kernel f(x) = x^(alpha-1) exp(-x), without 1/Gamma(alpha)
log_f_gamma <- function(x, alpha) (alpha - 1) * log(x) - x
### log of the Cauchy-shaped envelope g, which touches f at the mode alpha - 1
log_g_gamma <- function(x, alpha) {
    (alpha - 1) * (log(alpha - 1) - 1) - log(1 + (x - (alpha - 1))^2 / (2 * alpha - 1))
}
```

### Checking the envelope numerically

The proof uses the **unnormalized** $f$, and this matters. Up to a constant,
`log_g_gamma` is the log-density of $m + \sqrt{c}\,C$:

```{r}
#| label: verify-cauchy-link
x_check <- seq(0.1, 10, by = 0.37)
alpha_check <- 3.3
log_f_Y <- dcauchy((x_check - (alpha_check - 1)) / sqrt(2 * alpha_check - 1), log = TRUE) -
    log(sqrt(2 * alpha_check - 1))
range(log_g_gamma(x_check, alpha_check) - log_f_Y)   # constant across x confirms the claim
```

@tbl-envelope-threshold computes the minimum gap $\min_x \{\log g(x) - \log f(x)\}$
on a fine grid, both for the kernel $f$ used in the proof and for the
normalized density `dgamma` $= f/\Gamma(\alpha)$.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-envelope-threshold
#| tbl-cap: "Checks that the Cauchy envelope lies above the Gamma target, and shows that this depends on which version of the target is used.
#|   Minimum of log g(x) - log f(x) over x > 0, for several alpha. Negative means the envelope is violated somewhere.
#|   Against the kernel x^(alpha-1) exp(-x) the gap is never negative, as proved. Against the normalized
#|   density it is -log Gamma(alpha), which is negative for 1 < alpha < 2 because Gamma(alpha) < 1 there."
alphas_check <- c(1.1, 1.5, 1.9, 2.0, 2.5, 3, 4.5, 10)
xv <- seq(1e-6, 60, length.out = 2e4)
gap_kernel <- vapply(alphas_check, function(a) min(log_g_gamma(xv, a) - log_f_gamma(xv, a)), numeric(1))
gap_dgamma <- vapply(alphas_check, function(a) min(log_g_gamma(xv, a) - dgamma(xv, a, log = TRUE)), numeric(1))
knitr::kable(data.frame(alpha = alphas_check, gap_kernel = gap_kernel, gap_dgamma = gap_dgamma),
             digits = 5, col.names = c("alpha", "min gap vs kernel f", "min gap vs dgamma"))
```

The gap against the kernel is $0$ for every $\alpha$, attained at the mode,
exactly as the proof says. Against `dgamma` it equals $-\log\Gamma(\alpha)$.
That is negative for $1 < \alpha < 2$, so $g$ would *not* cover the normalized
density there. For $\alpha > 2$ it is positive, so $g$ still covers it but
with a wasted factor $\Gamma(\alpha)$, and the acceptance rate drops to
$1/A_g$ instead of $\Gamma(\alpha)/A_g$. The lesson is the one stated with
the algorithm: the inequality $g \ge f$ must hold for the functions
*actually used* in the ratio $f/g$. Here the right choice is the kernel,
which needs no $\Gamma(\alpha)$ at all.

### Sampling function

A batch-and-refill implementation is both clearer and much faster than
drawing one candidate at a time in an R loop: generate a vector of
candidates, vectorize the accept/reject test, keep the survivors, and top up
only the shortfall.

```{r}
#| label: gamma-sampler
sample_gamma_rej <- function(n, alpha, max_tries = 2e6) {
    out <- numeric(0); tries <- 0
    while (length(out) < n) {
        if (tries > max_tries) stop("acceptance rate too low: envelope is too loose")
        m <- n - length(out)
        x <- rcauchy(m) * sqrt(2 * alpha - 1) + (alpha - 1)
        tries <- tries + m
        x <- x[x > 0]                              # f = 0 for x <= 0: always rejected
        keep <- log(runif(length(x))) < log_f_gamma(x, alpha) - log_g_gamma(x, alpha)
        out <- c(out, x[keep])
    }
    structure(out[seq_len(n)], accept.rate = n / tries)
}
```

### Test cases and efficiency

```{r}
#| label: tbl-gamma-tests
#| tbl-cap: "Shows how the efficiency of the Gamma rejection sampler, measured by its acceptance rate, changes with the shape parameter.
#|   The simulated acceptance rate matches the exact rate A_f / A_g. It rises slowly with alpha
#|   towards 1/sqrt(pi) = 0.564, and the KS statistics show no departure from the Gamma distribution."
acc_theory <- function(a) exp(lgamma(a) - log(pi) - 0.5 * log(2 * a - 1) - (a - 1) * (log(a - 1) - 1))
set.seed(3)
alphas_test <- c(1.2, 2.5, 4.5, 20)
gamma_tests <- lapply(alphas_test, function(a) sample_gamma_rej(2000, a))
knitr::kable(data.frame(
    alpha = alphas_test,
    accept_theory = acc_theory(alphas_test),
    accept_rate = vapply(gamma_tests, attr, numeric(1), "accept.rate"),
    ks_stat = mapply(function(x, a) suppressWarnings(ks.test(x, "pgamma", a))$statistic,
                      gamma_tests, alphas_test)
), digits = 4, col.names = c("alpha", "exact acceptance", "simulated acceptance",
                             "KS statistic vs true Gamma"))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-gamma-tests
#| echo: !expr knitr::is_html_output()   # code shown in HTML only
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| fig-cap: "Verifies that the Gamma rejection sampler produces draws from the correct distribution.
#|   Q-Q plots of rejection-sampled draws against the true Gamma(alpha,1)
#|   quantiles, for three of the test cases: the envelope produces exact draws
#|   regardless of alpha, only the cost per draw changes."
par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
for (i in 1:3) {
    a <- alphas_test[i]
    qqplot(gamma_tests[[i]], rgamma(2000, a), xlab = "rejection sample", ylab = "rgamma sample",
           main = sprintf("alpha = %g (accept %.1f%%)", a, 100 * attr(gamma_tests[[i]], "accept.rate")))
    abline(0, 1, col = "firebrick", lwd = 2)
}
```

The Q-Q plots confirm exactness at every $\alpha$: rejection sampling never
trades accuracy for speed, only speed changes. About half of all proposals
are rejected for any $\alpha$, so this envelope is less efficient than the
Laplace envelope of Example 1. Efficient random-number generators for the
Gamma distribution (as used inside `rgamma` itself) use envelopes that are
much tighter; see Marsaglia & Tsang (2000, *ACM TOMS*) for the algorithm R
actually uses.

### Shinylive App for Rejection Sampling from a Gamma Density with a Cauchy Envelope {#sec-gamma-rejection-app}

There is a [shinylive app](../../shinylive_apps/app_gamma-rejection.html) to show how the efficiency of rejection sampling for the Gamma distribution changes with the shape parameter while the draws remain exact.

## Adaptive Rejection Sampling for Log-Concave Targets

Designing an envelope by hand, as above, is the hard part of rejection
sampling. For a broad and important class of targets it can be automated.

### Log-concavity and the tangent hull

A density $f$ is **log-concave** if $\log f(x)$ is concave. Many posteriors
are: the normal, the gamma with shape $\ge 1$, the beta with both parameters
$\ge 1$, logistic-regression posteriors under normal priors, and any product
of log-concave factors (so most conjugate and many non-conjugate exponential-
family posteriors qualify).

A concave function lies below every one of its tangent lines. So for tangent
lines $\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_k$ to $\log f$ at points $x_1 < \cdots < x_k$, the
piecewise-linear **upper hull**
$$
\log g(x) = \min_j \ell_j(x)
$$
satisfies $\log g \ge \log f$ everywhere, hence $g = e^{\log g} \ge f$: a
valid envelope, built automatically from a handful of tangent points and
their slopes (the log-density's derivative), with no hand-crafted formula.
Because $g$ is piecewise-exponential, both its normalizing integral and its
inverse CDF are closed-form on each piece, so sampling from $g$ is cheap.

::: {.proof}
**The tangent-line inequality.** Let $h = \log f$ be concave and
differentiable on an interval, and let $x_j$ and $x$ be two points in it. For
$t \in (0, 1]$, concavity gives
$h\big(x_j + t(x - x_j)\big) \ge (1-t)\,h(x_j) + t\,h(x)$, which rearranges to
$$
\frac{h\big(x_j + t(x - x_j)\big) - h(x_j)}{t} \ \ge\ h(x) - h(x_j).
$$
Letting $t \to 0$, the left side tends to $h'(x_j)(x - x_j)$, so
$h(x) \le h(x_j) + h'(x_j)(x - x_j) = \ell_j(x)$. This holds for every $j$,
so $h(x) \le \min_j \ell_j(x) = \log g(x)$ and $f \le g$.
:::

### The adaptive algorithm

**Adaptive rejection sampling** (Gilks & Wild, 1992) refines the hull as it
goes:

1. Start with a few tangent points, at least one on each side of the mode.
2. Draw $x \sim g$, $U \sim \text{Unif}(0,1)$; accept if $U < f(x)/g(x)$.
3. Whenever a point is **rejected**, add it to the tangent set and rebuild
   the hull.

Each rejection adds a tangent exactly where the envelope was loose, so the
acceptance rate rises toward $1$ as sampling proceeds — the envelope adapts
itself to the target instead of being fixed in advance. Only $\log f$ and its
derivative are required (a derivative-free variant uses secants in place of
tangents). The `ars` package implements this for any user-supplied
log-concave `f`.

## Example 3: Truncated Normal by Adaptive Rejection Sampling

The standard normal is log-concave ($\log f(x) = -x^2/2$ is concave), and
truncating to $[l, u]$ only shrinks the domain — it cannot break concavity —
so a truncated normal is log-concave too, and `ars` applies to it directly.
Explicitly, for $l < u$ (either may be infinite):

**Target.**
$$
f(x) = e^{-x^2/2}\,\mathbb{1}\{l < x < u\}, \qquad h(x) = \log f(x) = -\tfrac{x^2}{2} \ \text{ on } (l, u).
$$

**Envelope (ARS).** With tangent points $x_1 < \cdots < x_k$ in $[l, u]$, the
tangent at $x_j$ is
$$
\ell_j(x) = -\tfrac{x_j^2}{2} - x_j(x - x_j) = \tfrac{x_j^2}{2} - x_j x.
$$
Adjacent tangents $\ell_j$ and $\ell_{j+1}$ cross where
$\tfrac{x_j^2}{2} - x_j z = \tfrac{x_{j+1}^2}{2} - x_{j+1} z$, that is, at the
midpoint
$$
z_j = \frac{x_j + x_{j+1}}{2}, \qquad j = 1, \ldots, k-1.
$$
The envelope uses tangent $j$ between $z_{j-1}$ and $z_j$, with $z_0 = l$ and
$z_k = u$:
$$
g(x) =
\begin{cases}
\exp\big\{\tfrac{x_1^2}{2} - x_1 x\big\}, & l < x \le z_1, \\[4pt]
\exp\big\{\tfrac{x_2^2}{2} - x_2 x\big\}, & z_1 < x \le z_2, \\[4pt]
\qquad\vdots & \qquad\vdots \\[4pt]
\exp\big\{\tfrac{x_k^2}{2} - x_k x\big\}, & z_{k-1} < x < u.
\end{cases}
$$
Each piece is an exponential function of $x$, so $g$ is easy to integrate and
to sample piece by piece.

::: {.proof}
**$g \ge f$.** On the piece $z_{j-1} < x \le z_j$, $\log g(x) = \ell_j(x)$, and
$$
\ell_j(x) - h(x) = \tfrac{x_j^2}{2} - x_j x + \tfrac{x^2}{2} = \tfrac12 (x - x_j)^2 \ \ge\ 0.
$$
So $\log g \ge h$ on every piece, i.e. $g \ge f$ on $(l, u)$. This is the
tangent-line inequality above, verified directly. (This $g$ is the same as
the hull $\min_j \ell_j$: since $\ell_j(x) - \ell_{j+1}(x) = (x_{j+1} - x_j)(x - z_j)$,
tangent $j$ lies below tangent $j+1$ exactly when $x \le z_j$, so on each
piece the tangent in use is the lowest one.)
:::

This makes it a clean test case for comparing ARS against the most obvious
alternative: sample the *untruncated* $N(0,1)$ and throw away anything
outside $[l, u]$. That naive sampler is itself a (trivial) rejection
sampler, with envelope $g(x) = e^{-x^2/2}$ on all of $\mathbb{R}$. Here
$g \ge f$ because $f = g\cdot\mathbb{1}\{l<x<u\}$, and the ratio $f/g$ is $1$
inside $(l, u)$ and $0$ outside, so "accept if $U < f/g$" just means
"keep $x$ if it lands in $(l, u)$". It is exactly
correct — but its acceptance rate is just $P(l<Z<u)$, which collapses to
essentially $0$ once $[l, u]$ sits out in the tail. ARS has no such
weakness: its hull is built from the *truncated* target from the start, so
it never proposes a point outside $[l, u]$ in the first place, and its
acceptance rate stays high regardless of where the window sits.

```{r}
#| label: ars-fns
### direct rejection sampling for a truncated normal: draw from N(0,1),
### keep values inside [lb, ub]; vectorized batch-and-refill
sample_tnorm_drs <- function(n, lb = -Inf, ub = Inf) {
    out <- numeric(0)
    while (length(out) < n) {
        x <- rnorm(n - length(out))
        out <- c(out, x[x >= lb & x <= ub])
    }
    out
}

### adaptive rejection sampling via the ars package
sample_tnorm_ars <- function(n, lb, ub) {
    logf <- function(x) dnorm(x, log = TRUE)
    fprima <- function(x) -x
    ars(n, f = logf, fprima = fprima, x = c(lb, (lb + ub) / 2, ub),
        lb = TRUE, ub = TRUE, xlb = lb, xub = ub)
}
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ars-timing
#| tbl-cap: "Compares the cost of adaptive rejection sampling with that of naive rejection sampling for truncated normal distributions.
#|   Adaptive rejection sampling (ars) vs naive rejection sampling
#|   from an untruncated N(0,1): naive sampling degrades catastrophically
#|   as the truncation window moves into the tail, while ars does not,
#|   because it never wastes draws outside [lb, ub] in the first place."
set.seed(4)
n <- 1000
windows <- list(c(-5, -4), c(-50, -40), c(100, 110))
timing <- lapply(windows, function(w) {
    t_ars <- system.time(sample_tnorm_ars(n, w[1], w[2]))["elapsed"]
    t_naive <- if (w[1] > -10 && w[2] < 10) system.time(sample_tnorm_drs(n, w[1], w[2]))["elapsed"] else NA
    c(lb = w[1], ub = w[2], ars_seconds = t_ars, naive_seconds = t_naive)
})
knitr::kable(do.call(rbind, timing), digits = 4,
             col.names = c("lower bound", "upper bound", "ars (s)", "naive rejection (s)"))
```

For $[-50,-40]$ or $[100,110]$ the naive sampler's acceptance probability is
astronomically small ($P(-50<Z<-40) \approx 10^{-221}$), so it is left as
`NA` rather than run to timeout; `ars` samples these windows in a fraction of
a second because its envelope is built from the truncated density itself,
never from the untruncated normal.

```{r}
#| label: fig-ars
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| fig-cap: "Verifies that adaptive rejection sampling produces draws from the correct truncated normal distribution, even far out in the tail.
#|   Histograms of adaptive-rejection-sampled draws against the true
#|   truncated-normal density (red), in three increasingly extreme
#|   truncation windows: ars matches the target exactly regardless of where
#|   the window sits, only the cost per draw changes (@tbl-ars-timing)."
### log(pnorm(ub) - pnorm(lb)), numerically stable even when the naive
### difference underflows to 0 for windows far out in either tail
log_pnorm_diff <- function(lb, ub) {
    if (ub <= 0) {
        log_pu <- pnorm(ub, log.p = TRUE); log_pl <- pnorm(lb, log.p = TRUE)
        log_pu + log1p(-exp(log_pl - log_pu))
    } else if (lb >= 0) {
        log_su <- pnorm(ub, lower.tail = FALSE, log.p = TRUE)
        log_sl <- pnorm(lb, lower.tail = FALSE, log.p = TRUE)
        log_sl + log1p(-exp(log_su - log_sl))
    } else {
        log(pnorm(ub) - pnorm(lb))
    }
}
tnorm_density <- function(x, lb, ub) exp(dnorm(x, log = TRUE) - log_pnorm_diff(lb, ub))

par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
set.seed(5)
for (w in windows) {
    x <- sample_tnorm_ars(n, w[1], w[2])
    hist(x, breaks = 25, freq = FALSE, col = "steelblue", border = "white",
         main = sprintf("[%g, %g]", w[1], w[2]), xlab = "x")
    curve(tnorm_density(x, w[1], w[2]), add = TRUE, lwd = 3, col = "firebrick", n = 300)
    if (identical(w, windows[[1]])) {
        legend("topright", bty = "n", lwd = 3, col = "firebrick", cex = 0.8,
               legend = "true density")
    }
}
```

[]{#ars-app}A [shinylive app](../../shinylive_apps/app_ars_normal.html) runs this truncated normal example step by step. It shows how adaptive rejection sampling improves its envelope automatically, so that it becomes more efficient as sampling proceeds.

## Example 4: Gamma Distribution by ARS on $\log X$ {#sec-ars-loggamma}

The Gamma$(\alpha, 1)$ log density $(\alpha-1)\log x - x$ has second
derivative $-(\alpha-1)/x^2$, so it is concave only when $\alpha \ge 1$. For
$\alpha < 1$ the density is not log-concave (it rises to $\infty$ at $x=0$)
and ARS cannot be applied to $X$ directly. A change of variable fixes this.
Let $Y = \log X$. By the Jacobian $dx/dy = e^y$, $Y$ has density
$$
f_Y(y) \propto \exp\{h(y)\}, \qquad h(y) = \alpha y - e^y,
$$
with $h'(y) = \alpha - e^y$ and $h''(y) = -e^y < 0$. So $\log f_Y$ is concave
for **every** $\alpha > 0$.

**Target.** For $X$ truncated to $(l, u)$, with $a = \log l$ and $b = \log u$
(so $a = -\infty$ when $l = 0$ and $b = \infty$ when $u = \infty$),
$$
f(y) = \exp\{\alpha y - e^y\}\,\mathbb{1}\{a < y < b\}.
$$

**Envelope (ARS).** With tangent points $y_1 < \cdots < y_k$ in $(a, b)$, the
tangent at $y_j$ is
$$
\ell_j(y) = h(y_j) + h'(y_j)(y - y_j) = (\alpha - e^{y_j})\,y + e^{y_j}(y_j - 1),
$$
using $h(y_j) - y_j h'(y_j) = e^{y_j}(y_j - 1)$. Adjacent tangents $\ell_j$ and
$\ell_{j+1}$ cross at
$$
z_j = \frac{e^{y_{j+1}}(y_{j+1} - 1) - e^{y_j}(y_j - 1)}{e^{y_{j+1}} - e^{y_j}},
\qquad j = 1, \ldots, k-1.
$$
The envelope uses tangent $j$ between $z_{j-1}$ and $z_j$, with $z_0 = a$ and
$z_k = b$:
$$
g(y) =
\begin{cases}
\exp\big\{(\alpha - e^{y_1})\,y + e^{y_1}(y_1 - 1)\big\}, & a < y \le z_1, \\[4pt]
\exp\big\{(\alpha - e^{y_2})\,y + e^{y_2}(y_2 - 1)\big\}, & z_1 < y \le z_2, \\[4pt]
\qquad\vdots & \qquad\vdots \\[4pt]
\exp\big\{(\alpha - e^{y_k})\,y + e^{y_k}(y_k - 1)\big\}, & z_{k-1} < y < b.
\end{cases}
$$
Each piece is an exponential function of $y$. If $a = -\infty$, the first
piece must rise with slope $\alpha - e^{y_1} > 0$, i.e. $y_1 < \log\alpha$, so
that $g$ decays to the left. If $b = \infty$, the last piece must fall, i.e.
$y_k > \log\alpha$. Otherwise $g$ has infinite area and cannot be
normalized.

::: {.proof}
**$g \ge f$.** On the piece $z_{j-1} < y \le z_j$, $\log g(y) = \ell_j(y)$, and
$$
\ell_j(y) - h(y) = e^{y} - e^{y_j} - e^{y_j}(y - y_j)
= e^{y_j}\big(e^{t} - 1 - t\big), \qquad t = y - y_j,
$$
which is $\ge 0$ because $e^t \ge 1 + t$ for all $t$. So $\log g \ge h$ on every
piece, i.e. $g \ge f$ on $(a, b)$. (As in Example 3, this $g$ is the same as
the hull $\min_j \ell_j$: since
$\ell_j(y) - \ell_{j+1}(y) = (e^{y_{j+1}} - e^{y_j})(y - z_j)$, tangent $j$ lies
below tangent $j+1$ exactly when $y \le z_j$.)
:::

ARS can sample $Y$, and $X = e^Y$ is then an exact
Gamma draw. Truncating $X$ to $(l, u)$ just truncates $Y$ to
$(\log l, \log u)$, which keeps $h$ concave. With $l = 0$ the lower end is
$-\infty$, and the left tail of $Y$ is long when $\alpha$ is small: $h(y)
\approx \alpha y$ there, an exponential tail with the slow rate $\alpha$.

It is worth writing ARS out in full here. The `ars` package fails on this
target when $\alpha < 1$. For $\alpha = 0.3$ its draws of $\log X$ have
mean about $-5.3$ (over several seeds) instead of the true $E(\log X) =
\psi(0.3) = -3.50$, where $\psi$ is the digamma function. For $\alpha = 0.05$
it prints repeated internal errors (`ifault = 5`) and still returns biased
draws. Both problems seem to come from the long, nearly linear left tail of
$h$. The sampler below follows the three steps of the adaptive
algorithm above. Every rejected point becomes a new tangent. All areas and
inverse CDFs are computed on the log scale, so a piece with very little
mass cannot overflow or underflow. The squeeze test is left out for clarity,
so every proposal costs one evaluation of $h$.

```{r}
#| label: ars-loggamma-fns
### tangent-line hull for a concave h on (a, b); a = -Inf and/or b = Inf allowed.
### z holds the piece boundaries: a, the tangent intersections, b
build_hull <- function(ys, h, hprime, a, b) {
    ys <- sort(unique(ys)); hy <- h(ys); hpy <- hprime(ys); k <- length(ys)
    z <- c(a, numeric(k - 1), b)
    for (i in seq_len(k - 1))
        z[i + 1] <- (hy[i + 1] - hy[i] - ys[i + 1] * hpy[i + 1] + ys[i] * hpy[i]) /
                    (hpy[i] - hpy[i + 1])
    list(x = ys, hx = hy, hp = hpy, z = z)
}

### hull value at the two ends of each piece (-Inf at an infinite end,
### where the tangent slopes downhill), and log area under exp(piece)
piece_ends <- function(hull) {
    k <- length(hull$x)
    lo <- hull$hx + hull$hp * (hull$z[1:k] - hull$x)
    hi <- hull$hx + hull$hp * (hull$z[2:(k + 1)] - hull$x)
    lo[is.infinite(hull$z[1:k])] <- -Inf; hi[is.infinite(hull$z[2:(k + 1)])] <- -Inf
    cbind(lo, hi)
}
log_areas <- function(hull, v) {
    m <- pmax(v[, 1], v[, 2]); d <- pmin(v[, 1], v[, 2])
    flat <- abs(hull$hp) < 1e-10
    ifelse(flat, v[, 1] + log(diff(hull$z)), m + log1p(-exp(d - m)) - log(abs(hull$hp)))
}

### one draw from the normalized envelope: pick a piece in proportion to its
### area, then invert that piece's exponential CDF (on the log scale)
sample_hull <- function(hull) {
    v <- piece_ends(hull); la <- log_areas(hull, v)
    j <- sample.int(length(la), 1, prob = exp(la - max(la)))
    U <- runif(1)
    if (abs(hull$hp[j]) < 1e-10) {
        y <- hull$z[j] + U * (hull$z[j + 1] - hull$z[j]); logg <- hull$hx[j]
    } else {
        m <- max(v[j, ])
        logg <- m + log((1 - U) * exp(v[j, 1] - m) + U * exp(v[j, 2] - m))
        y <- hull$x[j] + (logg - hull$hx[j]) / hull$hp[j]
    }
    c(y = unname(y), logg = unname(logg))
}

### ARS for Y = log X, X ~ Gamma(alpha, 1) truncated to (l, u):
### h(y) = alpha*y - exp(y) is concave for every alpha > 0
ars_loggamma <- function(n, alpha, l = 0, u = Inf) {
    a <- log(l); b <- log(u); m <- log(alpha)       # m = mode of h
    h <- function(y) alpha * y - exp(y)
    hprime <- function(y) alpha - exp(y)
    ### starting points: an infinite end needs a tangent sloping downhill
    ### towards it, i.e. a point left of the mode if a = -Inf, right if b = Inf
    lo <- if (is.finite(a)) a else min(b, m) - 1
    hi <- if (is.finite(b)) b else max(a, m) + 1
    hull <- build_hull(lo + (hi - lo) * c(0.1, 0.5, 0.9), h, hprime, a, b)
    y <- numeric(n); got <- 0; proposed <- 0
    while (got < n) {
        d <- sample_hull(hull); proposed <- proposed + 1
        if (log(runif(1)) <= h(d["y"]) - d["logg"]) {
            got <- got + 1; y[got] <- d["y"]
        } else {                                   # rejected: add a tangent there
            hull <- build_hull(c(hull$x, d["y"]), h, hprime, a, b)
        }
    }
    list(x = exp(y), y = y, accept = n / proposed, tangents = length(hull$x))
}
```

@tbl-ars-loggamma checks the sampler on shapes well below and above $1$, with
and without truncation. The true truncated mean comes from the identity
$x\,\text{dgamma}(x;\alpha) = \alpha\,\text{dgamma}(x;\alpha+1)$, which gives
$$
E(X \mid l < X < u) = \alpha\,\frac{P_{\alpha+1}(l, u)}{P_\alpha(l, u)},
\qquad P_\alpha(l, u) = P(l < X < u),\ X \sim \text{Gamma}(\alpha, 1).
$$

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ars-loggamma
#| tbl-cap: "Verifies the ARS sampler on log X for truncated Gamma distributions, including shapes below 1 where the Gamma density itself is not log-concave.
#|   Each row uses 5,000 draws. The acceptance rate stays above 99% after only
#|   a dozen or two tangents, the sample means match the exact truncated means,
#|   and the Kolmogorov-Smirnov p-values show no departure from the target."
### P(l < X < u) for X ~ Gamma(alpha, 1)
p_trunc <- function(alpha, l, u) pgamma(u, alpha) - pgamma(l, alpha)
lg_cases <- list(c(0.05, 0, Inf), c(0.3, 0, Inf), c(0.3, 1, Inf), c(0.5, 0, 2),
                 c(2, 0.5, 3), c(5, 0, 1), c(1, 15, Inf))
set.seed(11)
lg_tab <- t(sapply(lg_cases, function(cc) {
    alpha <- cc[1]; l <- cc[2]; u <- cc[3]
    r <- ars_loggamma(5000, alpha, l, u)
    F_tr <- function(q) (pgamma(pmin(pmax(q, l), u), alpha) - pgamma(l, alpha)) /
        p_trunc(alpha, l, u)
    c(alpha = alpha, l = l, u = u, accept = r$accept, tangents = r$tangents,
      true_mean = alpha * p_trunc(alpha + 1, l, u) / p_trunc(alpha, l, u),
      sample_mean = mean(r$x), ks_p = ks.test(r$x, F_tr)$p.value)
}))
knitr::kable(lg_tab, digits = c(2, 2, 2, 4, 0, 4, 4, 3),
             col.names = c("alpha", "l", "u", "acceptance", "tangents",
                           "true E(X)", "sample mean", "KS p-value"))
```

@fig-ars-loggamma shows the draws for three of these cases on both scales.
On the $y$ scale every target is a smooth log-concave curve, even for
$\alpha = 0.3$, where the density of $X$ (bottom left) has a pole at $0$.
Truncation at $l = 1$ (middle) or to $(0.5, 3)$ (right) only cuts the
$y$-density at $\log l$ and $\log u$.

```{r}
#| label: fig-ars-loggamma
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6.2
#| fig-cap: "Verifies that sampling Y = log X by adaptive rejection sampling and returning X = exp(Y) gives exact draws from the truncated Gamma distribution, including for shapes below 1.
#|   Top: histograms of the ARS draws of Y = log X against the true log-concave
#|   density of Y (red). Bottom: the same draws transformed to X = exp(Y),
#|   against the truncated Gamma density. The bottom-left density has a pole at 0
#|   and is not log-concave, but the density of Y above it is."
fig_cases <- list(c(0.3, 0, Inf), c(0.3, 1, Inf), c(2, 0.5, 3))
set.seed(12)
draws <- lapply(fig_cases, function(cc) ars_loggamma(5000, cc[1], cc[2], cc[3]))
lab <- function(cc) sprintf("alpha = %g, (l, u) = (%g, %g)", cc[1], cc[2], cc[3])
par(mfrow = c(2, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 2.2, 1))
for (i in 1:3) {
    cc <- fig_cases[[i]]; P <- p_trunc(cc[1], cc[2], cc[3])
    hist(draws[[i]]$y, breaks = 30, freq = FALSE, col = "steelblue", border = "white",
         main = lab(cc), xlab = "y = log x", cex.main = 0.95)
    curve(exp(cc[1] * x - exp(x) - lgamma(cc[1])) / P, add = TRUE, lwd = 3,
          col = "firebrick", n = 400)
}
for (i in 1:3) {
    cc <- fig_cases[[i]]; P <- p_trunc(cc[1], cc[2], cc[3]); x <- draws[[i]]$x
    xmax <- quantile(x, 0.99)          # crop the long right tail for display
    hist(x, breaks = c(seq(cc[2], xmax, length.out = 30), max(x)), freq = FALSE,
         xlim = c(cc[2], xmax), col = "grey60", border = "white",
         main = lab(cc), xlab = "x = exp(y)", cex.main = 0.95)
    curve(dgamma(x, cc[1]) / P, from = max(cc[2], 1e-3), to = xmax, add = TRUE,
          lwd = 3, col = "firebrick", n = 400)
}
```

### Shinylive App for Sampling a Gamma Distribution by ARS on $\log X$ {#sec-ars-loggamma-app}

There is a [shinylive app](../../shinylive_apps/app_ars-loggamma.html) that runs this sampler one proposal at a time. You choose $\alpha \in (0, 5]$ and a truncation interval $(l, u)$. The app shows the tangent hull adapting to $h(y)$, and the histograms of $Y$ and $X = e^Y$ filling in. A sidebar table compares the running estimates of $E(\log X)$ and $E(X)$ with their exact values.

## Summary

- Rejection sampling turns draws from an envelope $g \ge f$ into *exact* iid
  draws from $f$, using only the ratio $f/g$; no normalizing constants are
  needed. The geometric view — uniform points under $g$, keep those under
  $f$ — explains why this works and why efficiency is exactly the ratio of
  the two areas.
- A good envelope is tight (high acceptance) and easy to sample; finding one
  by hand, as in the Cauchy envelope for the Gamma distribution above,
  requires matching the target's tails and curvature and can be delicate.
- Adaptive rejection sampling automates envelope construction for any
  log-concave target via tangent lines to $\log f$, tightening the envelope
  on every rejection.
- A target that is not log-concave can often be made so by a change of
  variable: the Gamma density with $\alpha < 1$ is not log-concave, but
  the density of $\log X$ is for every $\alpha$, so ARS on $\log X$
  followed by $X = e^Y$ gives exact Gamma draws.
- Limitations: an envelope with a bounded ratio $g/f$ may not exist when $f$
  has heavier tails than any convenient $g$, and in high dimensions the
  acceptance rate of a product envelope typically decays exponentially with
  dimension, for the same curse-of-dimensionality reason quadrature grids
  fail (Unit 8). These limitations motivate **importance sampling**, which
  reweights instead of rejecting, and **Markov chain Monte Carlo**, which
  builds a chain that adapts to the target as it runs — the subjects of the
  next two chapters.
